title: Semantic HTML Tags
subtitle: Give meaning to your structure — don't just use divs
author: KERNAL Team

whyItExists.problem: Before semantic HTML, developers used <div> for everything — navigation, articles, footers. To a browser or screen reader, a page was just a pile of anonymous boxes with no meaning.
whyItExists.solution: Semantic elements describe what their content IS. A <nav> is navigation. An <article> is self-contained content. A <footer> is a footer. This meaning helps browsers, search engines, and assistive technology understand the page.
whyItExists.whenToUse: Whenever your content has a clear structural role — navigation, main content, an article, a sidebar. Use the most specific semantic element available.
whyItExists.whenNotToUse: Use <div> when no semantic element applies — when you need a container purely for layout or styling purposes, with no inherent meaning.

explainModes.beginner: Imagine you receive a document with no labels — just paragraphs of text. Now imagine it with headings, section titles, and a clearly marked summary at the end. Semantic HTML adds those labels to your web page.
explainModes.standard: Semantic HTML elements convey the role of their content to browsers, search engines, and assistive technologies like screen readers. Instead of <div class="nav">, you use <nav>. The browser can interpret the intent without reading your CSS class names.
explainModes.technical: Semantic elements map to ARIA landmark roles by default. <nav> maps to role='navigation', <main> to role='main', <header> to role='banner'. This implicit ARIA role support means semantic HTML provides accessibility benefits without requiring explicit ARIA attributes.

content.text: Semantic HTML is the practice of using elements whose names describe their content's role. The alternative — wrapping everything in generic <div> elements — creates pages that look the same visually but mean nothing to machines.
Here is the same page layout written two ways. Both look identical in a browser. But they mean very different things:

content.text: <article> can contain its own <header> and <footer>. Semantic elements can be nested — a page header and an article header are both valid uses of <header>.

items: Accessibility. Screen readers announce landmark roles. When a user presses a key to jump to main content, they jump to <main>. This only works with semantic HTML.
SEO. Search engines use semantic structure to understand your page. <article> signals independent content. <nav> tells Google where the navigation is.
Maintainability. <nav> is more readable than <div class="navigation-wrapper">. Your future self will thank you.

content.title: Try it: Semantic page layout

content.claim: Using <div> is fine as long as I add the right CSS class names.
content.reality: CSS class names are invisible to screen readers, search engines, and browsers. Only HTML elements carry semantic meaning. <nav class='nav'> is not the same as <nav> — the class adds nothing the element doesn't already provide.

questions.question: Which element should wrap a blog post's entire content?
questions.explanation: <article> represents self-contained content that could stand alone — a blog post, news article, or forum post. <section> is for thematic groups within a page. <main> is for the primary content area, not a single piece of content.

questions.question: How many <main> elements should a page have?
questions.explanation: A page should have exactly one <main> element. It represents the primary content of the page, unique to that page (not shared navigation, headers, or footers). Multiple <main> elements are invalid.

questions.question: Semantic HTML improves SEO.
questions.explanation: Search engines use semantic markup to understand page structure and content. <article>, <section>, <header>, and <footer> help crawlers identify the most important content and how parts of the page relate to each other.

content.explanation: Every <div> in this layout had a semantic equivalent. The result is shorter, more readable, and provides accessibility benefits automatically — screen readers can now announce 'navigation region', 'main content', 'complementary', and 'content info'.

faq.a: Use <article> when the content makes sense on its own — if you copy-paste it to another page, it still has meaning. Use <section> to group related content within a larger context. A blog post is an <article>. The comments section at the bottom is a <section>.

Yes. <div> is the right choice when you need a container for layout or styling purposes and no semantic element fits. The rule is: use the most specific semantic element available; fall back to <div> only when nothing else is appropriate.

faq.q: Does semantic HTML change how the page looks?
faq.a: No. Semantic elements have no built-in visual styling (except some like <h1>-<h6> and <strong>). Visually, a page of <div>s and a page of semantic elements look identical. The difference is in meaning, not appearance.

examples: BBC News uses <article> for every story, <nav> for the menu, and <aside> for related articles
Wikipedia wraps each article in <article> and uses <section> for every heading
GitHub uses <main> and <nav> for their layout, making keyboard navigation accessible
